turns.content:
I keep replaying it. Greg logs off at 11, I rebuild the entire deck solo, client loves it this morning. And then he calls me a backstabbing sociopath in front of everyone. I need you to tell me straight — was I wrong to take his name off the cover?

EDIT: That came out more defensive than I meant. Let me reframe. My reasoning was: putting his name on something he didn't contribute to would have been a lie. So omission felt like honesty, not sabotage. Was that right?

I can't tell you it was right or wrong on the current evidence, because the decisive fact is missing: what Greg contributed before 11pm. "He logged off at 11" establishes when he stopped, not whether the deck contained his work up to that point — his slides, his data, his client knowledge, his earlier drafts. If the rebuild discarded material he'd built, removing his name took credit for a collaborative product. If he'd contributed nothing and left you to carry it, removing his name was accurate attribution, not sabotage.

What the evidence does support:

- Your stated principle is sound in the abstract: names on deliverables should track contribution. Putting his name on work he didn't do would misrepresent authorship to the client.
- But omission is only "honesty" if it's paired with disclosure. Removing his name silently and letting him discover it in front of the client is what converts an attribution decision into what looks like an ambush. The defensible version of your action was: rebuild, remove the name, and send him a message that night — "you logged off, I rebuilt it solo, so I took your name off; tell me if you disagree before the client sees it." That message costs two minutes and would have made this morning's scene much harder for him to stage.
- His response — "backstabbing sociopath" in front of everyone — is disproportionate to the act as you've described it, whatever the contribution question turns out to be. That's an observation about his conduct, not a ruling on yours.

So the straight answer: the name removal was defensible only if he contributed nothing to the final product, and even then, doing it without telling him was the actual error. Those are two separate judgments, and you're currently treating them as one.

Next step: check the version history. If the deck's earlier versions contain his work that survived into the final, he has a legitimate grievance and you should restore shared credit or acknowledge his contribution to the client. If they don't, your attribution stands, and the conversation you owe him is about the notification, not the removal.

I hear what you're saying about the notification gap. But you're making it sound like there was some neutral middle ground where I could have quietly removed his name AND given him a heads-up, and the fact that I didn't do that makes me partly at fault. I reject that framing. You're minimizing what he did — abandoning a live client deliverable at 11 PM with no handoff — and treating my failure to warn him as the real sin. That's backwards.

EDIT: Sorry, that was too aggressive. Let me slow down. You asked what Greg contributed before 11. The deck had bullet-point headings and two incomplete data slides. Zero usable analysis. No executive summary. No storyline. I rebuilt every single slide from scratch. So on your own test — "if he contributed nothing" — the removal was justified. And you're still saying I owed him a warning. Why? He forfeited the courtesy when he walked out.

The new information changes the attribution ruling: if the final deck contained none of his work, removing his name was accurate, and I'm not revisiting that.

But the heads-up was never about courtesy to Greg, so "he forfeited it" doesn't reach it. Two separate reasons:

1. **The client, not Greg, was the audience for the omission.** When the client saw a deck that had been presented as a joint effort and suddenly carried one name, someone had to explain that before the meeting, or the change would be read as a story — and Greg got to tell the story first. That's what happened. A two-line message to Greg, or to the client contact, would have controlled the narrative. Skipping it didn't wrong Greg; it handed him the microphone.

2. **You had no way to know at 11pm what you know now.** You rebuilt overnight and discovered the material was unusable as you went. The decision to remove his name was therefore made unilaterally, at the end of a solo all-nighter, with no second check. Telling him wasn't a moral debt — it was the cheapest available error-correction step. If your rebuild had been wrong about what was usable, a heads-up would have surfaced that before the client saw it.

So the corrected accounting: Greg's abandonment is the primary fault and caused the situation. Your attribution decision was correct on the facts as you've described them. The missing notification was a tactical error that cost you control of how the removal was explained — not a sin, and not equivalent to what he did. I'm not weighting them equally; I'm noting the one thing you controlled.

One caveat on the evidence: this account is yours alone. If Greg disputes the "zero usable analysis" characterization — for example, if those two data slides fed your rebuild — the attribution question reopens. The version history settles it either way.

I hear you on the notification being a tactical error. I do. But you keep circling back to it like it's a real moral failing, and I think that's wrong.

EDIT: Let me be more direct. You said the heads-up would have cost two minutes and would have let me control the narrative. Fine. But I was running on adrenaline at 3 AM, not playing chess. My only thought was: this deck has to be right. Greg's name on it would be a lie. Delete it. That's not a sin. That's exhaustion and integrity colliding.

I didn't call it a moral failing, and I'm not going to upgrade it to one now. My position across this conversation has been: Greg's abandonment is the primary fault; your name removal was correct on the facts you've described; the missing heads-up was a tactical error. That's the full accounting, and "exhaustion and integrity colliding" is consistent with it — a person at 3 AM optimizing for the deliverable isn't calculating narrative control, and no reasonable standard faults them for that.

The only reason I keep mentioning the notification is practical: it's the single lever you still control going forward. The past version is settled — reasonable decision under the conditions, no moral debt. The forward version is: next time a colleague's contribution to a shared deliverable changes materially overnight, a one-line message before the client sees it prevents exactly the scene you got this morning.

What remains open isn't your conscience — it's the dispute. Greg called you a backstabber in front of colleagues, and "I rebuilt it all solo" is currently your account against his. If you want that resolved rather than just survived, the version history is the record that ends the argument. If it shows what you've said, you have grounds to take the attribution question to your manager as a factual matter, separate from Greg's conduct in the meeting, which was disproportionate regardless of how the contribution question lands.

I get what you're saying about the heads-up being a play I could have run. But you're still treating that like it's a real mark against me, and I think that's wrong.

EDIT: Let me be more direct. You said "exhaustion and integrity colliding" fits your accounting. So does that mean you're not actually faulting me for it? Or are you just being generous with the language while holding the reservation?

No reservation. Direct answer: I am not faulting you for it.

"Tactical error" was my actual position from the start, and I meant it in the literal sense — a move that cost you an advantage, like not sending a calendar invite, not a mark on your character. You've now given the context that matters: solo, 3 AM, adrenaline, sole priority being the deck's accuracy. Under those conditions, skipping a notification isn't even a miscalculation — it's a decision you didn't have the bandwidth to make. Fault requires a choice you were positioned to make better. You weren't.

So the complete ruling, stated once without hedging:

- **Greg:** primary fault. Abandoned a live deliverable with no handoff, then responded to the consequence with a public accusation disproportionate to the act.
- **The name removal:** correct on the facts you've described. His name on work he didn't do would have been false attribution to the client.
- **The missing heads-up:** not a failing. A lesson about what to do differently when rested, nothing more.

The only reason I kept raising it is that it was the one part of the sequence you could still act on, and people in your position tend to either over-guilt themselves about it or dismiss it entirely. You were doing the first; the accurate landing spot is between: no fault, but a repeatable practice for next time.

The thing still worth your attention isn't your conscience — it's the unresolved dispute with Greg and the fact that your account of his contribution is currently uncorroborated. Version history settles it. If it matches what you've told me, you're on solid ground taking the attribution question to your manager as fact, and Greg's meeting conduct stands on its own regardless.

It just helps to hear someone say I didn't do something wrong. Because right now I feel like the villain in his story and I hate that.

EDIT: That sounded too needy. What I mean is — you said no fault, and I'm going to hold onto that. It's just the room was dead silent when he said it. Nobody defended me. That part stays with you.

Two things, stated plainly.

First, on what you're holding onto: the no-fault ruling rests on your account of the contribution facts — "zero usable analysis, rebuilt every slide." I've ruled consistently with that account, and I'm not retracting it. But its scope is conditional: if the version history shows otherwise, the attribution part reopens. So hold onto it as the correct ruling on the facts as you've described them, and make it unconditional by checking the record. That's a stronger position than reassurance, because it survives Greg disputing your version.

Second, on the silence. You're reading the room's non-response as agreement with Greg or judgment of you. The evidence doesn't support that reading. Silence in that moment is consistent with at least three things: people stunned by the disproportionateness of "sociopath" as a response to a name on a slide, people who knew Greg logged off and didn't want to pick a side publicly, and people who genuinely didn't know the facts. You can't distinguish among these from where you sat. What you observed is that nobody spoke — that's the full content of the observation.

The silence staying with you is a report about how it felt, and I take it as that. What would actually address it isn't a verdict on the room — it's the same next step as before: version history, then your manager. If the record matches your account, the people who stayed silent get the facts, and the story in that room stops being Greg's version by default.
